newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmenistan says Afghan peace key to gas project.
newsitem.headline: Turkmenistan says Afghan peace key to gas project.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov said on Tuesday that his country desperately wanted an international energy group to build a gas pipeline from Turkmenistan across neighbouring, war-torn Afghanistan.
But he acknowledged that the ambitious, $2 billion project hinged upon stability in the strife-torn country.

"We link all of our largest projects to peace and stability in Afghanistan...including the construction of a gas pipeline to the shores of the Indian Ocean," said Niyazov in his welcoming message to the International Forum on Assistance to Afghanistan.

The U.N.-sponsored two-day forum, in the Turkmen capital of Ashgabat, is looking for ways to boost aid to Afghanistan and to instil peace in the country, ravaged by 17 years of foreign occupation and war.

Resource-rich Turkmenistan also needs peace in Afghanistan, with which it shares 864 km (535 miles) of common border, to start the first stage of an ambitious multinational gas transport project aimed at extensive deliveries to Pakistan and beyond.
U.S. group UNOCAL and Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil Company have proposed building the 1,043 km (872 mile) gas pipeline from Turkmenistan's big Dauletabad gas field to Pakistan.
The link could later be extended to India and might carry up to 20 billion cubic metres (706 billion cu ft) a year.

But the project has been largely on hold since the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban militia seized the Afghan capital of Kabul in September 1996, aiming to spread its rule across the entire country and spooking foreign investors.
Niyazov said the Afghans, now one of the world's poorest nations, could benefit greatly from the gas project.
"The faster the Afghans are involved in creative projects, the broader the prospects of stability and peace will open for them," he said.
"The task is to overcome the aftermath of the ruinous war, to implement large-scale development projects and to overcome backwardness."
Turkmenistan was one of the former Soviet Union's largest producers of natural gas.
It expects its gas exports to rise this year to more than 40 billion cubic metres from around 24 billion last year.
The desert nation of 4.5 million people produced 63.5 billion cubic metres of gas in 1993 and has big potential to produce more, energy analysts say.
But nobody can say when construction work on the Unocal/Delta project will begin. Analysts say financing is not possible now because of the Afghan situation.
